beats.lead: America's first long-distance telegraph line was nearly buried.
beats.text: Morse started by laying the wire underground between Washington and Baltimore, using a plough built by Ezra Cornell.
beats.note: After about nine and a half miles, the line was failing. A partner had bought wire with defective insulation.

beats.text: Out of time, Morse took Cornell's advice and strung the wire overhead instead.
beats.note: Cooke and Wheatstone were already using poles in England.

beats.context: chestnut poles, about 300 feet apart, that replaced the buried pipe in the spring of 1844.

beats.text: On 1 May 1844, before the line was finished, it carried news of Henry Clay's nomination for president.
beats.note: 'What hath God wrought', sent on 24 May, was the official opening, not the first message.

beats.text: The phrase was not even Morse's choice. It was suggested by Annie Ellsworth, from the Book of Numbers.
beats.note: It arrived in Baltimore as dents in a moving strip of paper, not as sound.

beats.line: The famous first message was not the first message.
